lesson.title: Reading the Fine Print: Why Every Study Has Limits
lesson.summary: Teaches how to identify and state the real limitations of a study, especially bias, which no amount of extra data can repair, as distinct from ordinary sampling variability.
lesson.body:
Every study, no matter how carefully designed, has boundaries on what it can honestly claim. Being able to name those boundaries precisely, rather than waving at them with a vague phrase, is a skill of its own, and it is one graders and careful readers look for specifically.

Start with the distinction between an observational study and an experiment. An observational study watches individuals and records what they already were doing, so it can reveal an association between two variables but cannot by itself establish that one causes the other, because a lurking, or confounding, variable might be driving both. A study that finds people who exercise more also sleep better cannot conclude exercise causes better sleep, since something else, like overall health or stress level, could affect both variables at once. Only random assignment of a treatment in an experiment can rule out confounding on average by spreading its influence evenly across groups.

Then there is bias, a systematic tilt in how data was collected. Undercoverage leaves part of the population with no chance of being selected. Non-response bias appears when the people who do not respond differ in relevant ways from those who do. Response bias comes from how a question is worded or who is asking it. Voluntary response bias comes from letting people opt themselves into a sample. All of these push an estimate in a consistent direction, and here is the point that gets missed most often, on an exam and in the news alike, increasing the sample size does not reduce bias. A larger biased sample is still biased, it is simply a bigger, more confidently wrong number, because the margin of error only accounts for random sampling variability, never for a flaw built into the collection method itself.

Picture an online poll where a website invites any visitor to vote on a policy question and collects 50,000 responses overnight. Despite the huge n, this suffers voluntary response bias, since people with strong opinions are far more likely to click, and the reported margin of error is essentially meaningless because it describes sampling variability that was never the real problem. A properly randomized phone or mail survey of just a few hundred people, even with its wider margin of error, is the more trustworthy number, because its uncertainty is honestly quantified rather than hidden behind an impressively large sample size.

When you write up limitations, be specific. Do not write there could be bias or the sample size was too small as a generic hedge covering every possibility. Name the actual weak point, who was left out, how the question was worded, why respondents might not answer honestly, and if you can, say which direction it likely pushed the estimate. Also keep limitations separate from the variability already captured by the margin of error or confidence interval, restating that number is not a limitation, it is simply part of the reported uncertainty the study is already accounting for.
